test_text.title: A second attempt at domesticating the tomato

article.title: A second attempt at domesticating the tomato
glossary: * mutations: changes in an organism's genetic structure that can be passed down to later generations

items.sentence_raw: It took at least 3,000 years for humans to learn how to domesticate the wild tomato and cultivate it for food.
items.explain: Q17: The question asks for a comparison between early domestication and recent research. The passage says early domestication *'took at least 3,000 years'* but now teams *'have done it all over again in less than three years'* — this directly compares the old slow way with the new fast way. This is in section **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Now two separate teams in Brazil and China have done it all over again in less than three years.
items.explain: Q17: The question asks for a comparison between early domestication and recent research. The passage says early domestication *'took at least 3,000 years'* but now teams *'have done it all over again in less than three years'* — this directly compares the old slow way with the new fast way. This is in section **A**.

items.sentence_raw: And they have done it better in some ways, as the re-domesticated tomatoes are more nutritious than the ones we eat at present.

This approach relies on the revolutionary CRISPR genome editing technique, in which changes are deliberately made to the DNA of a living cell, allowing genetic material to be added, removed or altered.
The technique could not only improve existing crops, but could also be used to turn thousands of wild plants into useful and appealing foods.
In fact, a third team in the US has already begun to do this with a relative of the tomato called the groundcherry.
This fast-track domestication could help make the world's food supply healthier and far more resistant to diseases, such as the rust fungus devastating wheat crops.
"This could transform what we eat," says Jorg Kudla at the University of Munster in Germany, a member of the Brazilian team.
"There are 50,000 edible plants in the world, but 90 percent of our energy comes from just 15 crops."
items.explain: Q23: The question says humans use only a small proportion of available plant food. The passage quotes Kudla saying *'90 percent of our energy comes from just 15 crops'* out of *'50,000 edible plants'* — this means we use only a tiny fraction. So the answer is **A** (Jorg Kudla).

items.sentence_raw: "We can now mimic the known domestication course of major crops like rice, maize, sorghum or others," says Caixia Gao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing.
"Then we might try to domesticate plants that have never been domesticated."
Wild tomatoes, which are native to the Andes region in South America, produce pea-sized fruits.

Over many generations, peoples such as the Aztecs and Incas transformed the plant by selecting and breeding plants with mutations* in their genetic structure, which resulted in desirable traits such as larger fruit.
But every time a single plant with a mutation is taken from a larger population for breeding, much genetic diversity is lost.
items.explain: Q15: The question asks about problems from focusing only on a certain type of tomato plant. The passage explains that when you take *'a single plant with a mutation'* for breeding, *'much genetic diversity is lost'* and *'desirable mutations come with less desirable traits'* — this is exactly how problems arise. This is in section **B**.

items.sentence_raw: And sometimes the desirable mutations come with less desirable traits.
items.explain: Q15: The question asks about problems from focusing only on a certain type of tomato plant. The passage explains that when you take *'a single plant with a mutation'* for breeding, *'much genetic diversity is lost'* and *'desirable mutations come with less desirable traits'* — this is exactly how problems arise. This is in section **B**.

items.sentence_raw: For instance, the tomato strains grown for supermarkets have lost much of their flavour.
items.explain: Q24: The question asks for an undesirable trait caused by a mutation. The passage gives an example: tomato strains *'have lost much of their flavour'* — **'lost'** means it is an undesirable trait. So the answer is **'flavour'**.

items.sentence_raw: By comparing the genomes of modern plants to those of their wild relatives, biologists have been working out what genetic changes occurred as plants were domesticated.
The teams in Brazil and China have now used this knowledge to reintroduce these changes from scratch while maintaining or even enhancing the desirable traits of wild strains.
Kudla's team made six changes altogether.
For instance, they tripled the size of fruit by editing a gene called FRUIT WEIGHT, and increased the number of tomatoes per truss by editing another called MULTIFLORA.
items.explain: Q25: The question says modifying one gene made the tomato three times its original something. The passage says they *'tripled the size of fruit'* by editing a gene — **'tripled'** means made three times bigger. So the answer is **'size'**.

items.sentence_raw: While the historical domestication of tomatoes reduced levels of the red pigment lycopene - thought to have potential health benefits - the team in Brazil managed to boost it instead.
The wild tomato has twice as much lycopene as cultivated ones; the newly domesticated one has five times as much.
"They are quite tasty," says Kudla.
items.explain: Q18: The question asks for a personal reaction to the flavour of a genetically edited tomato. The passage quotes Kudla saying *'They are quite tasty'* and *'A little bit strong. And very aromatic'* — this is his personal opinion about the taste. This is in section **C**.

items.sentence_raw: The team in China re-domesticated several strains of wild tomatoes with desirable traits lost in domesticated tomatoes.
In this way they managed to create a strain resistant to a common disease called bacterial spot race, which can devastate yields.
items.explain: Q14: The question asks for a tomato that can resist a dangerous infection. The passage says researchers *'created a strain resistant to a common disease called bacterial spot race'* — **'resistant to a common disease'** means it can fight off a dangerous infection. This is in section **C**.

items.sentence_raw: They also created another strain that is more salt tolerant - and has higher levels of vitamin C.
items.explain: Q26: The question asks for something the tomato was not badly affected by, and was rich in vitamin C. The passage says they created a strain that is *'more salt tolerant - and has higher levels of vitamin C'* — **'salt tolerant'** means not badly affected by salt. So the answer is **'salt'**.

items.sentence_raw: Meanwhile, Joyce Van Eck at the Boyce Thompson Institute in New York state decided to use the same approach to domesticate the groundcherry or goldenberry ("Physalis pruinosa") for the first time.
This fruit looks similar to the closely related Cape gooseberry ("Physalis peruviana").
Groundcherries are already sold to a limited extent in the US but they are hard to produce because the plant has a sprawling growth habit and the small fruits fall off the branches when ripe.
Van Eck's team has edited the plants to increase fruit size, make their growth more compact and to stop fruits dropping.
"There's potential for this to be a commercial crop," says Van Eck.
But she adds that taking the work further would be expensive because of the need to pay for a licence for the CRISPR technology and get regulatory approval.
items.explain: Q22: The question says present domestication efforts are limited by costs. The passage quotes Van Eck saying taking the work further *'would be expensive because of the need to pay for a licence'* — **'expensive'** means the costs are a limit. So the answer is **C** (Joyce Van Eck).

items.sentence_raw: This approach could boost the use of many obscure plants, says Jonathan Jones of the Sainsbury Lab in the UK.
But it will be hard for new foods to grow so popular with farmers and consumers that they become new staple crops, he thinks.
items.explain: Q20: The question says unusual plants may not be accepted on a large scale. The passage quotes Jonathan Jones saying *'it will be hard for new foods to grow so popular... that they become new staple crops'* — **'hard to grow so popular'** means large-scale acceptance is unlikely. So the answer is **D** (Jonathan Jones).

items.sentence_raw: The three teams already have their eye on other plants that could be "catapulted into the mainstream", including foxtail, oat-grass and cowpea.
items.explain: Q16: The question asks for examples of plants not cultivated now but useful as food. The passage lists *'foxtail, oat-grass and cowpea'* as plants that could be *'catapulted into the mainstream'* — **'catapulted into the mainstream'** means they are not widely grown now but could become common foods. This is in section **E**.

items.sentence_raw: By choosing wild plants that are drought or heat tolerant, says Gao, we could create crops that will thrive even as the planet warms.
items.explain: Q19: The question says domestication could help plants adapt to future environmental challenges. The passage quotes Gao saying we could create crops that *'will thrive even as the planet warms'* — **'thrive even as the planet warms'** means adapting to future climate challenges. So the answer is **B** (Caixia Gao).

items.sentence_raw: But Kudla didn't want to reveal which species were in his team's sights, because CRISPR has made the process so easy.
items.explain: Q21: The question says it is not advisable to make future research direction public. The passage says Kudla *'didn't want to reveal which species were in his team's sights'* — **'didn't want to reveal'** means he thinks it is not good to make it public. So the answer is **A** (Jorg Kudla).
